clue.text: In conclusion, there are no secrets

definitions.meaning: first meaning: taking everything into account, as a summing-up phrase
second meaning, read literally: every single thing has been told

explanation.surface: Someone wraps up an inquiry by declaring that nothing remains hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works once as an idiom and once taken word for word: if everything is told, nothing is secret.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means 'in total, on balance', which is how a speaker sums up at the close of an argument.

clue.text: Complaint of mogul upset about arts degree

indicators.note: 'about' means going round, so the jumbled letters surround the degree
something upset is knocked out of its proper order, so the letters of the tycoon word are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written; rearranged it splits around the degree
Bachelor of Arts, the standard first degree in arts subjects

explanation.surface: A media tycoon grumbles about a degree course in the arts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' sounds like a grievance, but it is meant in the medical sense of an ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint can be an illness; this one is pain in the lower back.

clue.text: Island leads in trying out new green actions

indicators.note: the leads of words are the letters at their fronts, so only initials of the following words are used

parts.note: the opening letter of each of these five words

explanation.surface: An island community experiments with new environmental measures.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a Pacific island kingdom, so it serves as an example of an island.

clue.text: Flat patch in flight coming down

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the level area between two flights of stairs
second meaning: an aircraft arriving back on the ground

explanation.surface: An aeroplane's descent hits a smooth stretch partway through the journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' pulls towards aircraft, which the second meaning reinforces, but the first meaning is a flight of stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A staircase has a level platform between runs of steps, and an aircraft's arrival on the ground carries the same name.

clue.text: Gallery for queen in London museum

indicators.note: 'in' places one item inside another, so the royal goes within the museum's letters

parts.note: the V and A, the Victoria and Albert Museum in South Kensington
Elizabeth Regina, the usual crossword abbreviation for a queen

explanation.surface: A gallery is set aside for a queen in one of London's museums.
explanation.walkthrough: The V and A is the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, written out as V AND A.
explanation.definitionFit: A gallery can be a roofed platform along the outside of a house, which is exactly this open porch.

clue.text: Progress can almost go either way

parts.words: Progress can almost go either way
parts.note: surface reading: an advance might easily slip back as well as forward
setter's reading: the word reads nearly the same forwards and backwards, only its two middle letters swapping

explanation.surface: A cautious remark that advances are fragile and could just as easily reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards the answer gives EVLOVE: all but the central pair of letters match, so it is almost a palindrome.
explanation.definitionFit: To evolve is to develop gradually, so the verb is a synonym for making progress.

clue.text: Short and curly

parts.note: surface reading: echoes the idiom 'the short and curlies', hair one can be grabbed by
setter's reading: a symbol that is shorthand for the word 'and', and is drawn with curves

explanation.surface: Evokes the British phrase 'got by the short and curlies', meaning firmly trapped.
explanation.walkthrough: The & sign stands in for the word 'and' and is a curly character.
explanation.definitionFit: The symbol & abbreviates the conjunction 'and', and its shape is a looping flourish.

clue.text: See Canterbury or York, say

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a bishop's seat or district of authority
second meaning: these are the two archbishoprics of the Church of England, examples of the thing

explanation.surface: An invitation to visit one of two famous English cathedral cities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a verb telling you to visit, but it is the noun for a bishop's territory.
explanation.definitionFit: A see is the area under a bishop's jurisdiction; Canterbury and York are the two archbishops' territories in England.

clue.text: Daft description of Maradona's 1986 goal?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: struck with the knuckle while pretending to use the head

explanation.surface: Someone calls a famous World Cup goal stupid.
explanation.walkthrough: In the 1986 World Cup Maradona punched the ball in against England, the 'Hand of God' goal, passing it off as a header.
explanation.definitionFit: A knucklehead is a dolt, so the adjective means foolish; split up, it describes a ball put in by the hand rather than the head.

clue.text: Last word in alpha males

parts.note: alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, the equivalent of A
men are adult males

explanation.surface: Dominant men always insist on having the final say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alpha males' reads as one phrase, but the two words each give a separate piece; 'Last word' defines the word that ends a prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: This word is spoken at the close of a prayer or hymn, so it is literally the final word said.

clue.text: Idiot of an Ulster sergeant makes start on deck

parts.note: Northern Ireland, often called Ulster
a non-commissioned officer

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so just the first letter of that word is used

parts.note: the first letter of this word
the poop deck is the raised deck at a ship's stern

explanation.surface: A foolish army sergeant from Northern Ireland begins work on a ship's deck.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a jokey word for a silly, foolish person, a synonym of fool.

clue.text: Dreadful malaise almost cured by Italians

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter
something dreadful is in a terrible state, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: A terrible sickness is nearly healed by Italian doctors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cured' looks medical, following malaise, but it means preserved with salt; the definition is a description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a salted, air-dried sausage, a meat preserved in the Italian manner.

clue.text: Insure rent comforts retired person

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for a noun: something that keeps warm a person who has gone to bed

parts.note: to insure something is to cover it against loss
to let a property is to rent it out

explanation.surface: Paying rent and insurance gives peace of mind to a pensioner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' looks like a pensioner, but here it means gone to bed for the night.
explanation.definitionFit: A coverlet is a bedspread, which warms and soothes someone who has turned in.

clue.text: Assessor rejecting second mineral that is not what it seems

definitions.text: mineral that is not what it seems

parts.note: surface reading: a valuer turning down a second item brought before them

parts.words: mineral that is not what it seems
parts.note: setter's reading: a valuer would dismiss this on a second look because it only imitates the precious metal

explanation.surface: A valuer turns down a second-rate stone that looked more promising than it was.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay here is loose: the first half pictures an expert assessor rejecting the mineral on a second look, and the second half defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron pyrites glitters like the precious metal and has fooled prospectors, so it is a mineral that deceives.

clue.text: Community in toxic lake end up getting blood disorder

indicators.note: 'in' places the community inside the scrambled letters
something toxic is poisoned and spoilt, so the letters of the body of water are spoilt into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged around the community
the European Union, formerly the European Community

indicators.note: in a down entry 'up' means read from the bottom, so that word runs backwards

parts.note: an end can be a goal or purpose

explanation.surface: Pollution in a lake leaves a community ill with a disease of the blood.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a cancer of the white blood cells, so it counts as a disorder of the blood.

clue.text: Shake ladder: when centre pivots, he can't climb it

indicators.note: something that pivots swings round to face the other way, so those letters are read right to left
the centre of a phrase is its middle stretch, so the letters lie inside the words, spanning the gap

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second, read in the clue's order

explanation.surface: Wobble a ladder at its midpoint and someone will be unable to get up it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition rests on the old joke that these Doctor Who robots cannot climb stairs, let alone a ladder.
explanation.definitionFit: These pepper-pot alien villains from the BBC series Doctor Who glide on wheels and were long mocked for being unable to manage steps.

clue.text: Outcome of digital interaction with strings

definitions.text: Outcome of digital interaction with strings

parts.note: surface reading: sounds like the result of something done on a computer or online
setter's reading: fingers (digits) brushing across a guitar's strings

explanation.surface: Sounds like computing jargon about strings of characters in software.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital' means done with the fingers, not with computers, and 'strings' are those of a guitar, not text.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweeping the fingers across a guitar's strings produces this casual rhythmic sound.

clue.text: Aye, Scot slurred, that'll cover the brew

indicators.note: slurred speech runs words together indistinctly, so these letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tipsy Scotsman mumbles agreement while reaching for the pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brew' is British slang for a pot of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: This knitted or padded cover is put over a teapot to keep the drink inside warm.

clue.text: Bronze flooring makes the odds worse for blackjack punters

definitions.text: makes the odds worse for blackjack punters

parts.note: a bronze medal is awarded for third place
a deck is the floor of a ship or a raised wooden platform

explanation.surface: Someone describes a casino's bronze-coloured floor that somehow hurts gamblers' chances.
explanation.walkthrough: Adding more packs of cards to the shoe makes card counting harder, so a further pack worsens the players' odds.
explanation.definitionFit: In blackjack each extra pack shuffled in slightly raises the house edge, so another pack disadvantages gamblers.

clue.text: Prize for learning method with fixed core

indicators.note: 'with' says the method word holds the fixed one along with it
a core is the middle of something, so the fixed piece goes into the centre of the method word

parts.note: learning by rote means by repetition
set means fixed or established

explanation.surface: An award is given for a teaching technique built on a solid foundation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Core' tells you where the fixed piece goes: at the very centre of the learning method.
explanation.definitionFit: A rosette is a ribbon badge awarded as a prize at shows and competitions.

clue.text: Mousier? The opposite — more bitchy!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the reverse of more mouse-like is more cat-like
second meaning: more spiteful in speech

explanation.surface: Someone compares a timid person with a nastier one.
explanation.walkthrough: Cats are the opposite of mice, so the word works literally; the dog-related 'bitchy' adds a further joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Catty means spiteful and malicious in speech, so the comparative means more spiteful; literally it is more feline.

clue.text: The other overweight verger

parts.note: 'a bit of the other' is British slang for sex
a ton is a great weight, hence a huge amount over the limit

explanation.surface: An unusually heavy church official is singled out among others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The other' is a coy British euphemism for sex, from 'a bit of the other'.
explanation.definitionFit: A verger is a church caretaker, and this is another name for a similar church officer who looks after the building and graveyard.

clue.text: A late nap upset this smoker

definitions.note: a smoke rather than the person smoking it: a type of cigar

indicators.note: upset means overturned and disordered, so the letters are put into a new sequence

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tobacco lover is irritated at dozing off late in the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoker' looks like a person, but it is the thing smoked, a long thin cigar.
explanation.definitionFit: A panatela is a long, slender cigar, something lit and puffed by a smoker.

clue.text: Calm during closed debate

indicators.note: closed points to the close, or end, of each word, so only their closing parts are used

parts.note: taken as written; only its closing letters are kept
taken as written; only its closing letters are kept

explanation.surface: A private debate stays peaceful behind closed doors.
explanation.walkthrough: A loose clue: the answer is the last three letters of each of the final two words joined together.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedate describes a quiet, composed, unhurried manner, a synonym for being tranquil.

clue.text: Believer — in the lower social classes?

parts.note: D and E are the lowest grades in the British social classification of occupations
read as 'one who believes in', which the suffix -ist denotes

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a religious person comes from the working classes.
explanation.walkthrough: Britain grades households A, B, C1, C2, D, E by occupation; a DE-ist would be a believer in the bottom grades.
explanation.definitionFit: A deist believes in God from reason alone, without revealed religion, so is a kind of believer.

clue.text: Something the can be avoided by confirmed bachelors in their right minds?

definitions.text: Something the can be avoided by confirmed bachelors in their right minds

parts.words: Something the can be avoided by confirmed bachelors
parts.note: surface reading: the long-term pledge of marriage that lifelong single men steer clear of
setter's reading: anyone sane also avoids being sent to a psychiatric hospital

explanation.surface: A wry observation that sensible bachelors dodge marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue prints 'the' where 'that' is meant. The second sense is being sent to a mental hospital, which sane people escape.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a binding pledge like marriage and formal confinement in an asylum.

clue.text: Plant emerges, when it rains regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Flowers come up after regular rainfall.
explanation.definitionFit: The iris is a flowering garden plant with sword-shaped leaves, a member of the plant kingdom.

clue.text: Why noise in radio creates oppression

indicators.note: 'in' puts the sound inside the radio word

parts.note: old British slang for a portable transistor radio

indicators.note: a noise is a sound, so the question word is taken for how it sounds when spoken

parts.note: the letter Y is pronounced the same as the question word

explanation.surface: A puzzled listener asks why static on the radio feels like persecution.
explanation.walkthrough: The radio word is dated British slang for a pocket transistor set.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyranny is cruel and unjust rule, so it is a synonym for oppression.

clue.text: Apprentice drops in plate

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it go, so the little word 'in' is let go from the apprentice word

parts.note: an indenture is the contract binding an apprentice, and to indenture someone is to take them on as one

explanation.surface: A trainee knocks something into a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plate' sounds like crockery but is the dentist's word for the base holding false teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: A denture is a set of false teeth on a dental plate, so the two words name the same appliance.
